readings.reading: Christ was enthroned on the heavenly Zion at his resurrection and ascension (Hebrews 12:22) and reigns now. The nations' rebellion continues throughout this age, and the rod of iron describes his final judgment at the return, as well as the present triumph of his people (Revelation 2:26-27).
readings.support: The New Testament applies the psalm to the crucifixion, resurrection and exaltation, which places the king's installation in the past and the judgment in the future, without an intervening millennium.
readings.objection: Postmillennialists argue that this underplays the promise of the nations as an inheritance; premillennialists argue that it removes the earthly dimension of the rule from Zion.

readings.reading: Christ was declared Son at the resurrection, but his rule over the nations with a rod of iron awaits his return and the millennial kingdom, in which the saints share it (Revelation 2:26-27). The psalm thus spans the first and second advents.
readings.support: Revelation 2:26-27 promises the overcomers authority over the nations with an iron rod, which premillennialists read as their reign in the millennium after the return (Revelation 20:4).
readings.objection: Amillennialists argue that Revelation 2:27 describes the saints sharing Christ's victory, already begun, not a future earthly reign.

readings.reading: Classical dispensationalists hold that Christ is not yet reigning on David's throne on Zion; the installation and rod of iron are fulfilled at the Second Coming, when he rules the nations from Jerusalem in the millennium. Progressive dispensationalists (Bock, Blaising) argue that the Davidic reign was inaugurated at the resurrection (Acts 2; 13), with the earthly rule from Zion still future.
readings.support: The psalm speaks of an earthly Zion and of crushing the rebellious nations, which dispensationalists argue has not happened yet.
readings.objection: Critics say the New Testament's own use of the psalm (Acts 4:25-27; 13:33) places the installation at the resurrection, and Hebrews 12:22 identifies the Zion of the new covenant as heavenly.

readings.reading: The rulers raging against the anointed include Herod, Pilate and the leaders of Israel (Acts 4:25-27). The warning of 2:12 (that his wrath is quickly kindled) was carried out against unbelieving Jerusalem in AD 70, and the Son continues to receive the nations in the gospel age.
readings.support: Acts 4 explicitly applies 2:1-2 to the first-century authorities, and Jesus warned those same authorities of imminent judgment (Matthew 23:36).
readings.objection: Critics say the psalm's horizon is universal (all the nations, the ends of the earth), so AD 70 is at most a partial instance, not the fulfilment.

title: Sit at My Right Hand
summary: The LORD says to David's Lord, “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool.” The LORD will extend his mighty sceptre from Zion; he rules in the midst of his enemies; his people offer themselves willingly in the day of his power; he is a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek, and will shatter kings and judge among the nations. It is the Old Testament text most often quoted or alluded to in the New Testament.
keyIssue: What happens during the session at the right hand. The New Testament places Christ's enthronement at his ascension (Acts 2:34-36; Hebrews 1:13; 10:12-13). The question is whether the subduing of enemies “until” the footstool is complete happens progressively during this age, all at once at the return, or after the return in a millennium.

readings.reading: Christ is now seated at the right hand and will remain there until his enemies are made his footstool. He rules “in the midst of his enemies” (110:2), and his people volunteer freely in the day of his power (110:3). The subjugation of enemies therefore happens in history, through the gospel, before he returns, and his return comes after that victory.
readings.support: Hebrews 10:12-13 pictures Christ seated, waiting until his enemies are made a footstool, which places their subjugation during the session. Paul uses the same psalm to describe the reign that ends in the end (1 Corinthians 15:25).
readings.objection: Amillennialists answer that the enemies are made a footstool in a final, decisive act at the return (compare 2 Thessalonians 1:7-9), not by gradual conversion of the world. Rule “in the midst of enemies” suggests ongoing opposition.

readings.reading: Christ's session at the right hand is his present messianic reign, the millennium of Revelation 20. He rules now from the heavenly Zion through his word and Spirit, in the midst of enemies who will finally be subdued at his return and the last judgment. The psalm leaves no room for another reign after his return; at that point he hands the kingdom to the Father (1 Corinthians 15:24-28).
readings.support: Acts 2:34-36 announces Christ's enthronement as fulfilling the psalm, and Peter connects it with David's throne (Acts 2:30), which makes the present session the promised messianic reign.
readings.objection: Postmillennialists argue that this does not take seriously the progressive conquest implied in the psalm. Premillennialists argue that the session at the right hand is distinct from Christ's own kingdom on earth.

readings.reading: Christ reigns now at the right hand, which is a real inauguration of his kingdom. The subjugation of his enemies will be completed in stages: at his return he will judge the nations and reign on earth (110:5-6), and at the end of the millennium the last enemy, death, will be destroyed.
readings.support: The psalm moves from session (110:1) to judgment of kings and nations (110:5-6), which premillennialists see as a sequence beginning with the session and ending with a visible conquest, matching Revelation 19-20.
readings.objection: Critics argue that 1 Corinthians 15:25-26 places the destruction of death at the end of the session, so there is no period after the session in which death continues.

readings.reading: Classical dispensationalists (Walvoord) distinguish the Father's throne, where Christ sits now as priest, from the Davidic throne he will occupy on earth after his return; the rule from Zion (110:2) is millennial. Progressive dispensationalists (Bock) accept that the Davidic reign was inaugurated at the ascension, according to Acts 2:30-36, but hold that its fulfilment on earth, in relation to Israel and the nations, is still future.
readings.support: Revelation 3:21 distinguishes Christ's throne from his Father's throne. The psalm's concrete judgment of kings and nations awaits his visible return.
readings.objection: Critics argue that Acts 2 applies the psalm to Christ's present reign as David's heir, which makes a separate future Davidic throne unnecessary.

readings.reading: The session ended in AD 70, when his enemies (unbelieving Jerusalem and the old covenant order) were made his footstool and the day of his wrath (110:5) came. Christ reigns over a kingdom now fully established.
readings.support: Full preterists connect Jesus' warning to the high priest (Mark 14:62, citing Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13) with the judgment within that generation.
readings.objection: Critics argue that death, the last enemy, has not been abolished, and that Paul places the subjugation of all enemies (including death) at the general resurrection.

title: The Mountain of the LORD's House
summary: “In the latter days” (beʾacharit hayyamim) the mountain of the LORD's house will be established as the highest of the mountains. All nations will stream to it to learn God's ways; instruction (torah) will go out from Zion; he will judge between the nations, and they will beat their swords into plowshares and learn war no more. Micah 4:1-3 has the same oracle.
keyIssue: When the latter days are and what the mountain is. The New Testament says the last days began with Christ (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2). The question is whether the oracle is fulfilled progressively in the church now, in a literal millennial Jerusalem after the return, or in the final new creation.

readings.reading: The latter days began with Christ's first coming. The mountain is the exalted kingdom of God, the heavenly Zion to which the church has come (Hebrews 12:22), and the nations are now streaming to it through the gospel. As this continues, the word of God will increasingly shape nations and international relations, bringing a real, if not perfect, era of peace before Christ returns.
readings.support: The New Testament places the latter days in the present (Acts 2:17; 1 Corinthians 10:11). The picture is of nations being taught and changed, not destroyed, which suits gradual conversion; judgment and peace come through instruction going out from Zion, which matches the Great Commission going out from Jerusalem (Luke 24:47).
readings.objection: Critics say the world has not seen a general end to war in the two millennia since, and amillennialists say the perfect peace described points to the new creation rather than to a stage in history.

readings.reading: The prophecy is fulfilled in the church (spiritual Zion) as people from all nations come to Christ now, and is consummated in the new heavens and new earth, where war is no more. It does not describe an intermediate millennial age with a rebuilt Jerusalem.
readings.support: Hebrews 12:22 identifies Zion with the heavenly city that believers have already come to, and Revelation 21-22 pictures the nations walking in the light of the city in the new creation.
readings.objection: Premillennialists say the oracle describes a period in which nations still need judging and arbitration (2:4), which does not fit the eternal state. Postmillennialists say amillennialism postpones its historical aspect too much.

readings.reading: The prophecy partly began with the gospel's spread, but its picture of universal peace among nations who still need arbitration (2:4) fits best the earthly reign of Christ after his return, before the eternal state.
readings.support: The oracle includes nations being judged and taught, which implies a world where sin is still present but restrained. That is what premillennialists expect in the millennium.
readings.objection: Amillennialists answer that the prophets regularly describe the eternal state with imagery from their own world, so arbitration between nations need not imply continuing sin.

readings.reading: This is a literal prophecy of the millennial kingdom. Physical Mount Zion in Jerusalem will be elevated (compare Zechariah 14:10), the millennial temple will be there, and the nations will come to Jerusalem to be taught by the Messiah reigning on David's throne, while war ceases worldwide.
readings.support: The oracle uses specific geographic terms (Zion, Jerusalem, the house of the God of Jacob), and the companion passage Micah 4 adds that each will sit under his vine and fig tree, which implies an earthly, agricultural setting.
readings.objection: Critics argue that the New Testament reinterprets Zion and the temple in terms of Christ and the church (John 2:19-21; Hebrews 12:22), so a physical temple centre would reverse that fulfilment.

readings.reading: The “latter days” are the last days of the old covenant age, from Christ to AD 70 (Hebrews 1:2; 9:26). After the earthly temple was removed, the true house of the LORD, Christ and his church, was established as the chief mountain, and from then on the nations stream into it.
readings.support: The New Testament writers speak of living in the last days in their own time (Acts 2:16-17; 1 Peter 1:20), and the destruction of the old temple cleared the way for the new.
readings.objection: Critics argue that New Testament “last days” describe the whole period from Christ's first coming to his second, not only the forty years to AD 70.

title: The Increase of His Government
summary: A child is born and a son given, on whose shoulder the government rests; he is called Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God (ʾel gibbor), Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. “Of the increase (marbeh) of his government and of peace there will be no end”, on the throne of David, established with justice and righteousness forever. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this.
keyIssue: When the child sits on David's throne and what “increase without end” means: continual growth of Christ's present reign through history, the eternal reign that begins at his return, or a literal Davidic throne in Jerusalem after the return. Matthew 4:15-16 applies Isaiah 9:1-2 to Jesus' Galilean ministry, and Luke 1:32-33 echoes 9:7.

readings.reading: The child is Jesus, who took up David's throne at his resurrection and ascension. His government will increase continually and without end, starting from small beginnings and growing through history, which is how postmillennialists read the progress of the gospel. The guarantee is the zeal of the LORD of hosts (9:7), not human effort.
readings.support: Marbeh speaks of increase or growth, not mere duration, which matches the kingdom parables of growth (Matthew 13:31-33). The throne of David is linked to Christ's resurrection and enthronement (Acts 2:30-31).
readings.objection: Critics say that “no end” may describe the permanence of the kingdom rather than continuous growth in history, and that the history of the church shows decline as well as growth.

readings.reading: This prophecy is fulfilled in Christ's present reign on David's throne at the Father's right hand, which expands as the gospel goes to the nations and lasts eternally. There is no separate future Davidic reign in Jerusalem; the eternal kingdom begun at the first advent is consummated at the return.
readings.support: The prophecy emphasises the eternal (“forever”), not a thousand-year reign, and the New Testament presents the risen Christ as already on David's throne (Acts 2:30-36; 13:34).
readings.objection: Premillennialists argue that the throne of David is a specific, earthly throne in Jerusalem, so heaven cannot be its location.

readings.reading: The child is Jesus, and his rule was inaugurated at his exaltation, but the full, visible reign of justice and peace on David's throne will appear when he returns to reign on earth, and it will continue without end into the eternal state.
readings.support: The promise of justice and peace established on David's throne describes a visible order on earth, which premillennialists think the present age does not fulfil.
readings.objection: Amillennialists answer that the eternal character of the reign does not fit a limited millennium, and postmillennialists that it fits the present reign.

readings.reading: The birth was fulfilled at the first advent, but the reign on David's throne is future: Christ will sit on David's literal throne in Jerusalem in the millennium and reign forever. Between the two lies the church age, which the prophet did not see. This is a classic case of prophetic “gap”.
readings.support: Luke 1:32-33 promises Jesus the throne of his father David and a reign over the house of Jacob, which dispensationalists take as national and literal. Jesus did not reign over Israel in that sense at his first coming.
readings.objection: Critics argue that Peter in Acts 2:30-36 says Christ was raised and exalted precisely to sit on David's throne.

readings.reading: Christ's government was fully established in AD 70 when the old covenant age ended, and it now increases forever; there is no future consummation in which the kingdom changes.
readings.support: Full preterists see the present eternal reign without end as the kingdom fully come, which fits the endless increase of 9:7.
readings.objection: Critics argue that the full justice and peace described is not present in the world, and that the view leaves no future for the bodily resurrection confessed in the creeds.

title: New Heavens and a New Earth
summary: God announces that he creates new heavens and a new earth; Jerusalem will be a joy; weeping will not be heard. Yet the passage goes on to say that one who dies at a hundred will be considered young, and the sinner who reaches a hundred is accursed (65:20). People will build and plant and enjoy their work; the wolf and the lamb will feed together (65:25).
keyIssue: The passage calls itself “new heavens and a new earth” but still includes death, sinners and a long lifespan. Is this the eternal state described in the language of Isaiah's time (with long life as a picture of no death), a millennial kingdom with death still present, or the new covenant era (the gospel age), which partial preterists and postmillennialists call the “new creation” already begun?

readings.reading: This is the new creation already begun in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17), described in the gospel age as it reaches maturity. Because death and sin still exist, it cannot be the eternal state. It describes the long-term flourishing of Christ's kingdom in history, with prosperity, long life, peace and justice increasing as the gospel transforms society.
readings.support: Death and sinners are present (65:20), which excludes the eternal state; but the passage also calls itself new creation, which fits the new covenant era inaugurated by Christ.
readings.objection: Amillennialists answer that Revelation 21:1-4, which takes up this prophecy, applies it to the eternal state with no death. Premillennialists answer that the passage describes conditions after a decisive divine intervention, not a gradual process.

readings.reading: This is the eternal state, but Isaiah describes it in the terms of his own time: a lifespan of a hundred years would be extraordinary to the original hearers, a way of saying death has lost its power. Revelation 21:1-4 confirms that the reference is to the consummated new creation, and the fulfilment begins with Christ's first advent.
readings.support: Isaiah himself calls the scene new heavens and a new earth (65:17; 66:22), and Revelation 21 takes it up for the eternal state. Prophetic language naturally pictures the future in present-day images.
readings.objection: Premillennialists and postmillennialists argue that a sinner dying at a hundred cannot describe a world without sin and death; reading it as symbolic seems to evade the text.

readings.reading: The passage describes the millennial kingdom, in which life is long but death and sin are not yet removed, a stage before the eternal state that only premillennialism has a place for. Grudem lists Isaiah 65:20 among the main Old Testament supports for a future millennium.
readings.support: The conditions (death, but at an advanced age; a curse on sinners; animals at peace) fit neither the present age nor the eternal state, which suggests an intermediate earthly kingdom.
readings.objection: Critics answer that the passage itself calls the period “new heavens and new earth”, which Revelation 21 uses for the eternal state, so splitting the passage between millennium and eternity is hard to justify.

readings.reading: Many dispensationalists (Walvoord, Pentecost) take 65:17-19 as looking to the eternal state and 65:20-25 as describing the millennial kingdom, centred on Jerusalem, with long life and restored nature. Others read the whole passage as millennial, with the eternal state as its final form.
readings.support: The presence of death, building, planting and childbirth requires an earthly, pre-eternal kingdom in which Israel is restored in its land.
readings.objection: Critics argue that a shift from the eternal state to the millennium mid-passage has no textual marker, and that the passage is consistent if read either as a single picture of the consummation or as a picture of the present age.

readings.reading: The new heavens and new earth are the new covenant order that replaced the old covenant world (Hebrews 8:13). It was established in Christ and confirmed when the old order ended in AD 70. It then develops in history, which is why death and sin can still appear in it. A final consummation follows at Christ's return.
readings.support: Old Testament “heavens and earth” language can describe a covenant order (Isaiah 51:15-16; Deuteronomy 32:1), and the new covenant is new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17; Galatians 6:15).
readings.objection: Critics argue that 2 Peter 3:10-13 and Revelation 21 describe a cosmic renewal and the removal of death, which has not yet occurred, so the covenantal reading at most captures part of the meaning.

readings.reading: The new heavens and new earth of Isaiah 65 and Revelation 21 are the new covenant world, fully arrived in AD 70. There is no future cosmic renewal; the passage describes the present spiritual reality of the church.
readings.support: Full preterists argue that the passage itself shows that the new heavens and earth contain death and sin, which makes it the present age rather than a future perfect world.
readings.objection: Critics answer that Revelation 21:4 explicitly removes death, and that Romans 8:18-23 expects creation itself to be freed from corruption. They note that denying a future renewal departs from historic orthodoxy.
